title: Medication Safety Foundations

sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Compare spilling water on the kitchen floor with spilling water on a laptop. You probably spill about as often in either place, but only one spill destroys something. High-alert medications are the laptop. What earns a drug that label is not how often people slip up with it, but how bad the outcome is when they do. Once you see that the defining feature is consequence rather than frequency, the extra guardrails make sense: locked storage, pre-mixed concentrations, and a second person checking are all ways of buying down a very expensive outcome.

### Question 2

When two words open the same way, your eye reads the beginning and lets the rest blur. You see "predni-" and your brain declares the job finished. Tall man lettering interrupts that shortcut by capitalizing only the part that differs, the way a highlighter marks the single line on a page you must not skim. The endings, not the beginnings, are what actually separate these drugs, so the formatting drags your attention to where the real information lives.

### Question 3

Picture moving house twice in one week. Boxes get loaded, unloaded, and reloaded, and unless someone stands at the door comparing the inventory list to what actually came off the truck, items vanish quietly and duplicates pile up. Medication reconciliation is that person at the door: "You arrived on five medicines, these new orders list four and one at a different strength. Which is intended?" Every hand-off, admission, transfer, discharge, is a doorway, and doorways are exactly where things go missing.

### Question 4

Write a capital U and a zero side by side, quickly, the way anyone writes at 0300. Both are rounded loops, and when the U is jammed against the end of "10" it simply reads as one more digit. Nothing dramatic happens on the page; 10 quietly becomes 100. With insulin that is not a small overshoot, it is a dose that can drop blood sugar dangerously. The fix is deliberately low-tech: write the word "unit," because a word cannot be misread as a numeral.

### Question 5

A decimal point is a speck of ink, and specks disappear in faxes, photocopies, and hurried handwriting. So test each number by asking what survives if the speck vanishes. Lose the point in ".5 mg" and you are left with 5 mg, ten times too much. Lose it in "5.0 mg" and you are left with 50 mg, again ten times too much. The zero in front rescues the number; the zero on the end inflates it. That asymmetry is the whole rule: one zero is a seatbelt, the other is a trap door.

### Question 6

If someone tells you the answer is 42 before you work the problem, your mind stops solving and starts looking for reasons to agree. That is not a check, it is an echo. A real second check means the other clinician goes to the original order and the actual vial or bag, works it out cold, and only then compares. Two people who genuinely solved it separately can disagree, and disagreement is the entire point. Two people where one merely nodded along produced one answer wearing two signatures.

### Question 7

A barcode scan is a handshake between two things: this medication and this person. Tape a spare label to the cart and the scanner shakes hands with a piece of paper, and paper agrees with absolutely everything. The screen flashes green, the documentation looks flawless, and the dose can still walk into the wrong room. Nothing about the technology failed here; the loop it was quietly closing was cut open by the workaround, and the reassuring green light is no longer telling you the person in front of you is the right one.

### Question 8

Say hydroxyzine and hydralazine quickly and they collapse into the same sound; look at them on a shelf and they occupy the same visual space. One relieves itching and anxiety, the other lowers blood pressure, so the swap is not a minor variation on the intended therapy. That is what look-alike/sound-alike means: the mistake originates in the name itself rather than in the dose, the route, or the timing. Ask where the confusion started, and the classification answers itself.

### Question 9

A room number describes furniture, and furniture does not get discharged, transferred, or swapped at 0200, but patients do. Asking "You are Mr. Alvarez, right?" is worse still, because you have handed over the answer and invited a polite nod. So use an open question and match two facts that travel with the person, name and date of birth, against the record. Requiring two matches works the way a key plus a password works: either one alone is guessable, both together rarely line up by accident.

### Question 10

Telephones flatten sound, and "fifteen" and "fifty" arrive nearly identical. Repeating an order from memory replays your own mishearing back at the prescriber in the same distorted form, and asking a colleague to check your typing only proves you typed the mistake accurately. Writing it first and then reading it aloud gives the one person who knows what was intended a chance to hear the error while it is still fixable. Spelling the name and speaking digits separately removes the last two places where sound alone can betray you.

### Question 11

Draw two circles that partly overlap. One circle is "something went wrong in the process," the other is "a medicine hurt the patient." Many process failures are caught at the pharmacy or the bedside and never touch anyone, so they sit in the first circle alone. And a person can react badly to a drug that was chosen and given perfectly, which lands in the second circle with no mistake anywhere. Only the overlap is both harmful and preventable, and that slice is where safety work concentrates because it is the part anyone can actually shrink.

### Question 12

You can post a warning sign at the top of a staircase, or you can install a gate. The sign works only when a tired, distracted person happens to look up; the gate works even when nobody looks at all. Taking concentrated potassium off the unit is the gate, because no one can grab the dangerous vial by mistake when the dangerous vial is not in the building. Training and labels still matter, but they draw on attention and memory, and attention and memory are precisely what a hard shift spends first.
